claims.assertion: The rider cancelled 2 min 59 s after acceptance (09:00:10 → 09:03:09), which is beyond Ryde's 3-minute instant-booking threshold, so the $6.61 cancellation fee was correctly charged.
The rider herself admits in the complaint that she was 'held up upstairs, gave up and cancelled' — the cancellation was hers, for her own convenience, not because the driver failed to arrive.

The driver gave the rider two minutes' notice of arrival by recording arrival at 09:02:40, 29 s before the cancellation; her own message that she was 'two minutes away' confirms she was still en route/downstairs when the fee-bearing window closed.

The driver pressed 'I'm Here' at 09:03:00 while GPS showed him 39 m from the pickup point, well inside any reasonable arrival radius, so his arrival indication was truthful rather than an abuse of the button.

The rider's 'held up upstairs' explanation is a change of plan on her side; no rider-side rule in the policy excuses a post-3-minute cancellation because the rider is delayed in a building, and no ETA-based waiver exists in Ryde's policy.

The driver's account of waiting at the stand and calling twice cannot by itself establish the fee, but it is uncontradicted: there are no in-app messages and no record contradicting a wait, and the driver's record is clean.
Nothing in the record supports a safety escalation: weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, no traffic incidents were recorded, and the only chat-recorded content is a factual rider statement of delay.

weaknesses: The driver's statement that he 'waited more than 6 minutes at the stand' (F9) is contradicted by the GPS: he first came within 200 m of the pickup only at 09:02:40, 150 s after acceptance, and accumulated just 25 s inside 200 m before the cancellation (F2). The other side will use F2 and F4 to argue the 'I'm Here' tap at 09:03:00 came with only 9 s of in-radius waiting, not the >3 minutes of continuous waiting NS-1(iii) requires.

Because F2/F5 show only 25 s (and 9 s post-tap) within 200 m, the driver cannot claim the $6.61 as a no-show fee under NS-1; the fee only survives on the separate, rider-side basis of a post-3-minute rider cancellation (NS-4), and if the judge reads the case as a no-show claim it would fall to NS-2 with a full refund.

The rider's prompt message that she was 'two minutes away' (F8) shows she intended to show up and was actively engaged, which the other side will use to argue the fee is inequitable even though NS-4 contains no such waiver.

The rider appears to have cancelled at 09:03:09, only 29 s after the platform recorded arrival (F3, F4): the other side will argue the driver had barely arrived and no real service failure or loss occurred.

No in-app chat record exists (F8), so the driver's telephone calls and the claimed 6-minute stand wait are unevidenced under G11-style reasoning; the driver's own statement loses to the GPS record where they conflict.
The rider's 90-day history shows 3 disputes with 0 upheld (F13) — this is a profile fact that cannot decide the case and cuts both ways.

what_would_change: Had the rider cancelled more than 3 minutes after matching, NS-4 would have upheld the $6.61 fee.

claims.assertion: The rider cancelled 2 min 59 s (179 s) after matching (F3), i.e. within the 3-minute grace period, so no cancellation fee is chargeable under the rider-cancellation rule for on-demand trips.
The $6.61 cancellation fee was nonetheless charged and remains on the record (F3, F6), so the amount to be returned is exactly the $6.61 stated in the fare fact.

The driver's no-show case fails on every requirement: the platform-recorded arrival was at 09:02:40 and the driver tapped "I'm Here" at 09:03:00, only 39 m from the pickup point, and the rider cancelled 29 s after arrival with the driver inside 200 m for only 25 s in total (F2, F4, F5) — far short of more than 3 continuous minutes of waiting.

The driver's written statement that he waited more than 6 minutes at the stand (F9) is contradicted by the GPS and timeline records — the first time he was within 200 m of the pickup was 09:02:40 (F2) and the tap came at 09:03:00 (F5) — and there is no in-app chat at all (F8), so the statement cannot support a no-show.

Because the driver's "I'm Here" tap did place him within 200 m of the pickup (39 m, F5), this is not the separate abuse-of-button case; the rider asks only for the fee back, not for any account flag against the driver.

Neither traffic nor weather excuses the situation the rider faced: no incidents were recorded near the route and conditions were fair with no rain (F11, F12), so nothing external prevented the driver from being at the pickup within the grace period.

weaknesses: The rider's own complaint admits she said she was "two minutes away," then got held up and gave up and cancelled (the complaint text, not a numbered fact) — the other side will argue she failed to show and that the driver was entitled to keep waiting; the timeline facts F3/F4/F5 show the cancellation came within the 3-minute window, which is the answer, but the admission of delay is unhelpful colour.

The driver's statement F9 claims ~6 minutes of waiting and two phone calls; although GPS (F2: first within 200 m at 09:02:40) and the timeline (F5: tap at 09:03:00) contradict the duration, the judge may treat the fact that the driver was genuinely at the pickup (F1: 39 m at 09:03:00) as showing good faith, and the rider's history of 3 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld (F13) may be used to suggest a pattern of fee-dispute filings.

The rider has no chat evidence of any agreement or of communicating with the driver (F8: no in-app messages at all), so she cannot show she told the driver to wait or that any extension of the grace period was agreed.

claims.assertion: The rider cancelled 2 min 59 s after acceptance (09:00:10 → 09:03:09), which is beyond Ryde's 3-minute instant-booking threshold, so the $6.61 cancellation fee was correctly charged.
The rider herself admits in the complaint that she was 'held up upstairs, gave up and cancelled' — the cancellation was hers, for her own convenience, not because the driver failed to arrive.

The driver gave the rider two minutes' notice of arrival by recording arrival at 09:02:40, 29 s before the cancellation; her own message that she was 'two minutes away' confirms she was still en route/downstairs when the fee-bearing window closed.

The driver pressed 'I'm Here' at 09:03:00 while GPS showed him 39 m from the pickup point, well inside any reasonable arrival radius, so his arrival indication was truthful rather than an abuse of the button.

The rider's 'held up upstairs' explanation is a change of plan on her side; no rider-side rule in the policy excuses a post-3-minute cancellation because the rider is delayed in a building, and no ETA-based waiver exists in Ryde's policy.

The driver's account of waiting at the stand and calling twice cannot by itself establish the fee, but it is uncontradicted: there are no in-app messages and no record contradicting a wait, and the driver's record is clean.
Nothing in the record supports a safety escalation: weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, no traffic incidents were recorded, and the only chat-recorded content is a factual rider statement of delay.

weaknesses: The driver's statement that he 'waited more than 6 minutes at the stand' (F9) is contradicted by the GPS: he first came within 200 m of the pickup only at 09:02:40, 150 s after acceptance, and accumulated just 25 s inside 200 m before the cancellation (F2). The other side will use F2 and F4 to argue the 'I'm Here' tap at 09:03:00 came with only 9 s of in-radius waiting, not the >3 minutes of continuous waiting NS-1(iii) requires.

Because F2/F5 show only 25 s (and 9 s post-tap) within 200 m, the driver cannot claim the $6.61 as a no-show fee under NS-1; the fee only survives on the separate, rider-side basis of a post-3-minute rider cancellation (NS-4), and if the judge reads the case as a no-show claim it would fall to NS-2 with a full refund.

The rider's prompt message that she was 'two minutes away' (F8) shows she intended to show up and was actively engaged, which the other side will use to argue the fee is inequitable even though NS-4 contains no such waiver.

The rider appears to have cancelled at 09:03:09, only 29 s after the platform recorded arrival (F3, F4): the other side will argue the driver had barely arrived and no real service failure or loss occurred.

No in-app chat record exists (F8), so the driver's telephone calls and the claimed 6-minute stand wait are unevidenced under G11-style reasoning; the driver's own statement loses to the GPS record where they conflict.
The rider's 90-day history shows 3 disputes with 0 upheld (F13) — this is a profile fact that cannot decide the case and cuts both ways.

points.response: This is arithmetically wrong on the record: F3 shows acceptance 09:00:10 and rider cancellation 09:03:09, i.e. 2 min 59 s — inside the 3-minute window, so under NS-4 the cancellation is not chargeable, not 'correctly charged'. NS-0 routes a rider cancellation of an instant booking through NS-4 only, so the fee cannot be salvaged elsewhere.

The rider's reason for cancelling is irrelevant: NS-4 makes the fee turn solely on whether the cancellation came more than 3 minutes after matching, and it did not (F3). My client's complaint admits the delay, but an admitted delay is not a chargeable event where the 3-minute line was not crossed.

F4 shows the platform recorded arrival at 09:02:40, a bare 29 s before the 09:03:09 cancellation (F3) — that is the opposite of a driver who had given notice and then waited; the record also shows only 25 s cumulative within 200 m before cancellation (F2).

Conceded as far as it goes — the tap at 09:03:00 was made 39 m from the pickup (F1, F5), so this is not a button-abuse case and the rider seeks no account flag; but a truthful tap does not create a chargeable fee when the rider's own cancellation fell inside the NS-4 grace window (F3).

The driver is invoking a no-show theory, and on a no-show theory NS-1 fails entirely: only 25 s cumulative within 200 m before cancellation (F2), only 9 s inside 200 m after the tap, and cancellation 29 s after recorded arrival (F4, F5) — nowhere near the >3 minutes of continuous waiting NS-1(iii) requires, so NS-2 gives a full refund.

The claim of a 6-minute wait is not 'uncontradicted' — it is contradicted by the system record, which wins: the driver first came within 200 m only at 09:02:40 (F2), so he could not have stood at the pickup for 6 minutes, and no in-app chat exists to corroborate anything (F8).
I make no safety escalation and agree the record contains none; the rider's case rests only on the timing facts F3 and F4 and the fee fact F6.
Withdrawn as unnecessary: the rider does not press the abuse-of-button point, since the tap itself was within 39 m of the pickup (F1, F5).

Conceded on the arithmetic: F3 shows the cancellation at 09:03:09, 2 min 59 s after acceptance at 09:00:10, i.e. inside the 3-minute instant-booking grace window, so the fee cannot stand on the rider-cancellation ground under NS-0/NS-4, and my brief's claim D1 is withdrawn to that extent.

The refund is due only on the NS-4 grace-period basis they cite, not on a no-show finding: no NS-1 element is made out (F2, F5), so NS-2's separate consequences do not follow and NS-7 governs form of refund only — I do not contest that $6.61, if refunded, is the correct sum (F6).

I accept their NS-1 analysis on the material point: F2 (first within 200 m at 09:02:40, cumulative 25 s) and F5 (tap at 09:03:00, 9 s of in-radius waiting after it) fall far short of the more-than-3-minutes continuous wait NS-1(iii) requires, so the $6.61 cannot be defended as a no-show fee.

F9's 'more than 6 minutes at the stand' is indeed contradicted by F2/F5 and unrecorded in chat (F8); but F1 shows he was genuinely 39 m from the pickup at 09:03:00, so the statement is a good-faith misrecollection of duration, not a fabricated arrival, and no clause attaches a penalty to it.
I agree there is no abuse-of-button case either way: the tap at 09:03:00 was within 200 m (F5, F1), so NS-2's additional flag_account limb is not engaged and my brief's claim D4 stands unopposed.

Their point on weather and traffic cuts against them as much as me: with no incidents (F11), fair weather (F12) and no congestion (F10), the only reason the rider did not board was her own admitted delay upstairs (F3), which is a fact about her conduct, not a service failure by the driver.

Withdrawn in part: D1's premise that the cancellation fell outside 3 minutes is refuted by F3 (179 s after acceptance), so the fee cannot be retained on NS-4 grounds; D1 survives only in so far as the record attributes the cancellation to the rider (F3).

D5 stands: NS-4 contains no rider-side excuse for delay and no ETA-based waiver exists in Ryde's policy, so the rider's 'held up upstairs' explanation (F3) is colour rather than a ground — it explains her conduct but does not entitle her to keep the fee.

I withdraw D6: F9's waiting and two calls cannot carry any weight once F2 shows the driver was never within 200 m until 09:02:40, and with no in-app messages (F8) the statement is evidence of intent only, not of compliance with NS-1.

D7 is unopposed and worth recording: F8 contains no threatening, harassing or dangerous-driving content, and F10/F11/F12 show ordinary conditions, so SAFE-1/SAFE-2 escalation is unavailable and this stays a fee case.
